title: Stakeholder analysis, influence & engagement
blurb: Explain how analysing stakeholders tells you who to influence, how, and how closely to engage them, using the power/interest grid.
question: A council is redesigning its bin-collection routes. The project manager has listed 40 stakeholders and plans to send every one of them the same monthly newsletter. Why is this a weak approach, and how should stakeholder analysis shape the way each stakeholder is influenced and engaged?

teach.h: Understand first, then influence and engage
teach.body: Stakeholders are the individuals or groups who have an interest in the project, or who can affect or be affected by it. Stakeholder engagement is the systematic identification, analysis, planning and carrying out of actions designed to influence them. In plain English: find out who matters, work out what they care about and how much sway they have, then decide how to win and keep their support. Analysis comes first because you cannot influence someone you do not understand.

steps.label: Identify
steps.sub: Who is affected, who can affect us?

steps.label: Plan
steps.sub: Engagement plan: approach and level for each

steps.label: Review
steps.sub: Re-assess as interest and power shift

teach.caption: A typical stakeholder engagement process. Each step feeds the next, and the loop never really stops until the project closes.

cells.label: Keep satisfied
cells.sub: Meet their needs, don't overload them

cells.label: Manage closely
cells.sub: Key players: engage fully and often

teach.caption: Power (or influence) is the ability to change the project's course; interest is how much they care about or are affected by it. The quadrant sets how much engagement effort each stakeholder gets.

teach.h: Why analysis drives influence and engagement
teach.body: Analysis answers three questions: who to prioritise, what will move them, and how closely to engage. Power and interest show where effort pays off. Attitude shows whether you are building on support or overcoming resistance. Needs show which message and benefit will land. Skip the analysis and effort is spread evenly: key players are under-engaged and may block the project, while low-priority groups are swamped with information they don't want.

teach.h: What each analysis factor tells you
head: Factor
Question it answers
How it shapes engagement
rows: How much do they care or gain/lose?
How often and how much detail
Build on support or tackle concerns
What do they want from us?
Which message and benefit to stress

teach.h: Scenario: Northvale Council's new bin routes
teach.body: The cabinet member for environment controls funding but has little day-to-day interest: keep satisfied with short briefings. The refuse crews and their union have high power and high interest: manage closely through workshops on the new routes. Residents care a lot but individually have little power: keep informed by letter and website, with a feedback form. The routing software vendor is mostly unaffected: monitor. One newsletter for all 40 would suit none of them.

rows.label: Main analysis
values: At the start, light and frequent

rows.label: Re-analysed
values: At phase gates and big changes

rows.label: Typical level
values: Inform and consult, involve key players

teach.caption: Both need analysis; iterative work relies on users and the product owner giving feedback every time box, so engagement is closer and more frequent.

teach.text: Classic mix-up: high power + LOW interest is 'keep SATISFIED', not 'keep informed'. 'Keep informed' is for LOW power + HIGH interest. And the grid is a snapshot: a stakeholder can move quadrant as the project starts to affect them, so analysis must be repeated.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define the link: analysis gives the understanding that influence and engagement depend on.
Name what is analysed: interest, power/influence, attitude and needs.
Explain the grid: it prioritises effort (manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor).
Show the result: an engagement plan with the right approach, level and techniques per stakeholder.
Add that analysis is repeated, because power and interest change during the life cycle.
Analysis → influence → engagement: you cannot influence what you don't understand.
Analyse interest, power/influence, attitude and needs.
Grid: manage closely (high/high), keep satisfied (high power), keep informed (high interest), monitor (low/low).
The engagement plan sets each stakeholder's approach and level of engagement.
Revisit the analysis: positions move. Iterative projects engage users every iteration.

summary: You can now explain why stakeholder analysis must come before influence and engagement, and what interest, power, attitude and needs each reveal. You can also place stakeholders on the power/interest grid and say how that shapes the engagement plan in linear and iterative projects.

A.q: A regional operations director can stop the project's funding but rarely asks how it is going. Using a power/interest grid, how should the project manager treat this stakeholder?
A.why: High power with low interest is the 'keep satisfied' quadrant: meet their needs with concise updates so their support is kept without overloading them.

whyNot.0: Manage closely is for stakeholders with high power AND high interest.
whyNot.1: Keep informed is for low-power stakeholders with high interest.
whyNot.3: Monitoring suits low power and low interest; ignoring someone who controls funding is risky.

A.q: What is the main reason stakeholder analysis is carried out before the engagement plan is written?
options: It shows how and how much to engage each one
It records each stakeholder's contact details
It removes the need for later communication
It confirms which stakeholders back the sponsor
A.why: Analysis provides the understanding (interest, power, attitude, needs) that tells the project manager which approach, level and influencing techniques suit each stakeholder.

whyNot.1: Contact details may be recorded, but that is not the purpose of analysis.
whyNot.2: Analysis directs communication; it never replaces it.
whyNot.3: Support for the sponsor is only one aspect of attitude, not the main reason for analysis.

A.q: Which THREE of the following are typically assessed during stakeholder analysis? 1. Interest  2. Power or influence  3. Attitude to the project  4. Their job grade alone
A.why: Analysis assesses interest, power/influence, attitude and needs. Job grade alone says little: a junior person can still be very influential.

whyNot.0: Job grade alone is not a reliable measure; attitude is missing from this set.
whyNot.2: Interest is missing, and job grade alone is not an analysis factor.
whyNot.3: Power or influence is missing, and job grade alone is not an analysis factor.

B.q: Residents living next to a planned depot are very worried about noise but have no formal say in the decision. Where do they sit on the power/interest grid?
B.why: Low power with high interest means 'keep informed': give regular, clear updates and a route for their concerns, which also stops them building opposition.

whyNot.0: Keep satisfied is for high-power, low-interest stakeholders.
whyNot.1: Monitoring is for low interest; these residents are highly interested.
whyNot.2: Manage closely needs high power as well as high interest.

B.q: Complete the statement: stakeholder analysis ______ the choice of influencing approach and level of engagement.
B.why: Analysis informs influence and engagement: the understanding it produces is what those choices are based on.

whyNot.1: Analysis does not replace engagement; you still have to engage.
whyNot.2: Analysis comes before, not after, deciding how to engage.
whyNot.3: They are directly linked: that relationship is the point of LO 10a.

B.q: On a two-year hospital project, why should the stakeholder map be revisited at each phase gate?
options: Low-power groups must be removed at each gate
Each gate needs a brand-new stakeholder list
Interest and power shift as work moves on
B.why: As the project moves on, new groups are affected, people change roles and interest rises or falls, so positions on the grid change and engagement must adapt.

whyNot.0: There is no such rule; the map is updated, not banned.
whyNot.1: Low-power stakeholders are still monitored or kept informed, never simply removed.
whyNot.2: The list is updated, not rebuilt from scratch at every gate.

C.q: To be fair, a project manager gives every stakeholder the same time and the same updates. What is the most likely result?
options: Key players get too little; effort wasted
Every stakeholder ends up equally satisfied
Communication costs are kept to a minimum
C.why: Without prioritisation, high-power, high-interest stakeholders get too little attention and may block the project, while low-priority groups receive more than they need.

whyNot.1: Different stakeholders need different things, so identical treatment satisfies few of them.
whyNot.2: Engaging everyone equally usually costs more, not less.
whyNot.3: Resistance needs targeted influence based on understanding their concerns.

C.q: A software firm builds a new app in two-week iterations. How does stakeholder engagement typically differ from a linear project?
options: Users are only engaged at final acceptance
Stakeholder analysis is not needed at all
Users review and shape each increment
Only the sponsor is engaged in each iteration
C.why: Iterative life cycles depend on users and the product owner reviewing each increment and giving feedback, so engagement is continuous and often at the collaborate level.

whyNot.0: Engaging users mainly at acceptance is more typical of a linear life cycle.
whyNot.1: Analysis is still needed; it is simply revisited more often.
whyNot.3: Users and the product owner, not just the sponsor, are central in each iteration.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of stakeholder analysis?
options: It shows where engagement effort is best spent
It reveals likely resistance before it grows
It helps choose the message for each group
It ensures every stakeholder will agree
C.why: Analysis improves the odds of support, but no technique can guarantee every stakeholder will agree.

whyNot.0: Prioritising effort is a core benefit of analysis.
whyNot.1: Assessing attitude lets the project manager spot and address resistance early.
whyNot.2: Understanding needs and interests helps tailor the message.

reteach.title: Planning a family wedding
reteach.question: You are organising a wedding. Who gets a say in the menu, who just gets an invitation, and who do you keep sweet? How is that the same as stakeholder analysis?

blocks.body: The couple's parents are paying and care deeply: you involve them in big decisions (manage closely). A grandparent rarely asks questions but could veto the venue: you check in so they're happy (keep satisfied). Friends are excited and want news: you send updates (keep informed). The venue's neighbours barely notice: you just watch for issues (monitor). You only got this right because you first understood who cares and who has sway.

blocks.text: If the grandparent suddenly takes an interest in the guest list, they move to 'manage closely'. Positions change, so the analysis is repeated.

explain.body: A stakeholder is anyone with an interest in the project, or who can affect or be affected by it: sponsor, users, team, suppliers, regulators, the public. Missing one early is a common cause of late objections and rework, so use several sources: interviews, the business case, organisation charts and lessons learned.

test.q: Which group is LEAST likely to be overlooked as a stakeholder if the project only uses its own team's view?
test.why: A team working from its own view will always see itself; it is external groups such as regulators, residents and suppliers that tend to be missed.

whyNot.0: Regulators are external and often missed until they object.
whyNot.2: Residents are external and easily forgotten by an inward-looking team.
whyNot.3: Suppliers not yet appointed are easily overlooked.

explain.body: For each stakeholder, assess interest (how much they care or are affected), power or influence (whether they can change the project's course), attitude (supporter, neutral or resistant) and needs (what they want from the project). This is the understanding that influence depends on.

test.q: A project manager learns a powerful union representative is openly resistant. Which analysis factor has this revealed?
test.why: Resistance or support is the stakeholder's attitude to the project.

whyNot.1: Interest is how much they care or are affected, not whether they support it.
whyNot.2: Needs are what they want from the project.
whyNot.3: Power is already known here; the new insight is their resistance.

explain.body: Plot each stakeholder on the power/interest grid. High power, high interest: manage closely. High power, low interest: keep satisfied. Low power, high interest: keep informed. Low power, low interest: monitor. The grid turns analysis into priorities.

test.q: A supplier of office stationery has little interest in the project and little power over it. What is the right approach?
test.why: Low power and low interest is the 'monitor' quadrant: minimal effort, but watch in case their position changes.

whyNot.0: Keep informed is for high-interest stakeholders.
whyNot.1: Keep satisfied is for high-power stakeholders.
whyNot.3: Manage closely needs both high power and high interest.

explain.body: The engagement plan records, for each stakeholder, the aim, the level of engagement (inform, consult, involve or collaborate), the influencing techniques, who owns the relationship and how often. Engagement then happens, and the analysis is reviewed as the project moves on.

test.q: Which document turns the results of stakeholder analysis into agreed actions for each stakeholder?
test.why: The stakeholder engagement plan sets out the approach, level, techniques, owner and frequency for each stakeholder, based on the analysis.

whyNot.0: The risk register records uncertain events and responses.
whyNot.2: The business case justifies the investment.
whyNot.3: A benefits profile describes one benefit and how it will be measured.
